cases.testName: checkout.spec.ts > TC-CHK-03 non-USD currency > EUR price for a 1-9 cent product (Red Flashlight)

got.summary: GET /api/products?currencyCode=EUR returned 504 Gateway Timeout while checkout and product-catalog containers were unhealthy and 6 other api tests also failed with 504. The stack is broken, so this run says nothing about the EUR rounding behaviour the test targets.

evidence.why: The failure is an upstream gateway timeout, not a wrong price or assertion on business data.
Containers on the failing flow were unhealthy, so the results are untrustworthy.
Six sibling api tests failed with 504 in the same run, which indicates a wall of gateway errors, not a single product defect.
The diff only changes the README, so no code change could have caused the failure.

alternative.why_not: A 504 across many tests with unhealthy containers points to the stack, and the diff touches no product code. No wrong business value was observed, and no known defect (e.g. DEF-08) can be confirmed from a timeout.

next_action.detail: Investigate and restart the unhealthy checkout and product-catalog containers, confirm the stack is healthy, then rerun the whole api project. TC-CHK-03 covers money and currency, so check its result after the rerun and don't treat it as passing from this run.

cases.testName: cart.spec.ts > TC-CART-01 cart operations (API) > adding the same product twice merges the line

got.summary: The cart API call failed with ECONNREFUSED on 127.0.0.1:8080, and 12 other tests failed the same way. The frontend or proxy on port 8080 was most likely down or not listening, so this is a stack outage and not a cart bug.

evidence.why: The connection was refused at the TCP level, so no request reached the app and no cart logic ran.
There were 13 failures out of 49 executed tests, all with the same ECONNREFUSED error. That points to a shared cause and not one broken test.

alternative.why_not: The failure is not timing or shared state in this test. The port refused connections for many unrelated tests at once, and the diff is empty. A product bug is also ruled out because the cart logic never ran.

next_action.detail: Check that the frontend or envoy proxy is up and listening on port 8080, restart the Docker Compose stack, and rerun the suite. No container was reported unhealthy, so check the container logs for the cause of the crash or restart. Retrying alone is unlikely to help.

cases.testName: payment-failure.spec.ts > TC-PAY-04 injected payment failure > most orders decline when paymentFailure is on

got.summary: TC-PAY-04 got 0 declines on attempt 1, then 19 of 20 on retry. The flag paymentFailure was set about 1s before the first order and flagd evaluation was never polled, so the flag probably hadn't propagated yet. This looks like a test race, not a product bug.

evidence.quote: Note: flag paymentFailure set to 0.95 about 1s before the first order of attempt 1; flagd evaluation API not polled.
evidence.why: The test did not wait for the flag to take effect before placing orders, which is a timing race.

evidence.quote: Attempt 2 (passed): 19 of 20 orders declined with 422 PAYMENT_FAILED
evidence.why: With the flag in effect, the product declines orders as expected, so the product is right.
The test passed on retry with no code change, which fits a timing issue. The log shows no wrong business data, so it is not a DEF-10 style product bug.

alternative.why_not: The retry shows the product declines orders correctly with 422 PAYMENT_FAILED. The diff is empty, and the log has no wrong business data, no server-state-versus-UI mismatch and no known defect. The failure matches a flag propagation race.

next_action.detail: After setting paymentFailure, poll the flagd evaluation API until it returns the new value, and only then place orders. Do this instead of relying on a fixed delay. The test is a payment test, so a human may want to check that the 0-decline result was a propagation delay and not a real missed decline.

cases.testName: checkout.spec.ts > TC-CHK-01 happy path order (API) > order succeeds in USD

got.summary: The checkout API call returned 422 PAYMENT_FAILED on attempt 1 while a parallel flagd test had paymentFailure at 0.95. The flag was restored 800ms later and the retry passed. This is cross-test interference through shared stack state, so the test isolation is at fault. The product is behaving as configured.

evidence.quote: Run context: this spec ran in the 'api' project, in parallel with another worker finishing a flagd test that had paymentFailure at 0.95. Flag was restored by its test 800ms later.
evidence.why: A parallel test left the global paymentFailure flag on, which explains the payment failure.
The failure is the payment failure the flag injects, not wrong business data.
The test passed on retry once the flag was restored, which fits transient shared state.
The order succeeded once the flag was back to normal, so the product is correct.

alternative.why_not: No sibling failures and no unhealthy containers. The stack was healthy, and tests disturbing each other through a flagd flag is a test-isolation flaw (rule 6).

next_action.detail: Isolate the flagd paymentFailure test from the parallel api project. Run it serially or in a dedicated project, or give it its own flagd scope, and always restore the flag in a finally/afterEach block. Quarantine the flagd test until that is done. Confidence is medium because the 422 was not directly tied to the flag by a timestamp in the log, but the overlap is strong.

cases.testName: checkout.spec.ts > TC-CHK-02 displayed price equals charged price > Red Flashlight: order cost equals catalogue price

got.summary: The order cost came back as 57.8 instead of the catalogue price 57.08, which is the DEF-01 symptom. The diff changes how getDouble in the currency service reads nanos, and that code is on the failing price flow. Checkout money values are wrong, so this needs a human (S1).

evidence.why: The charged cost drops the leading zero of the cents (08 becomes 8). This is the DEF-01 signature, and the test assertion itself is correct.

evidence.quote: for (char c : std::to_string(m.nanos())) { frac += (c - '0') * scale; scale /= 10; }
evidence.why: to_string(nanos) has no leading zeros, so 80000000 and 8000000 give the same fraction. A value like .08 is read as .8 in this product code on the currency flow.

evidence.quote: DEF-01 (S1): Order cost differs from the displayed price ($57.08 shown, $57.80 costed)
evidence.why: This is the same price and the same symptom as the known defect.

alternative.why_not: The expected value of 57.08 is the correct catalogue price and the test has no locator or stale-annotation problem. The diff changes product source, not test code. The log shows a wrong money value.

next_action.detail: Link this to DEF-01 as an S1 defect. The getDouble change in src/currency/src/server.cpp parses std::to_string(m.nanos()) digit by digit, which drops leading zeros of the 9-digit nanos field (for example 8000000 is read as .8). Revert the change, or zero-pad nanos to 9 digits, or compute units + nanos / 1e9. Add a regression test for prices with 1-9 cents.
